subject: The Cultivation No-Dig bed, depicted in mid-July

generation.prompt:
Redraw this book illustration as a convincing unstaged photograph of a Cornish home garden in mid-July, landscape 3:2. There are three image inputs with different jobs. IMAGE 1, the last page 153 image, supplies the composition, bed and July brief only. Replace its visual rendering completely. IMAGE 2, DSC01820, is a real ordinary photograph from the same position during construction. It is the authority for the bed proportions and the garden behind it: the angled glazed greenhouse on its shallow weathered masonry base, blue shed edge, an old timber planter on short legs with a compact shrub and the mismatched terracotta pots to the left, black butt by the greenhouse, pale weathered fence. Use the photographic realism, scale and texture of this camera reference. IMAGE 3, DSC01959, is the real crop reference for grown lettuce and beetroot in this garden. Its low airy plants, uneven ground-level spread, loose clusters, overlaps, missed plants, handling marks and perspective are the authorities for the plants. Use that photograph's lighting, subdued greens and soil detail. Do not bring in its hoops, bright paving or adjacent vegetable beds, or the cardboard, foreground bricks, large barrel or adjacent crops from image 2.

Retain the closer view of the main no-dig bed. Show its whole 1.2 m wide, elongated rectangular footprint, seen obliquely from the near left with the long axis receding up to the right; both short ends and narrow grassy margins read clearly within the frame. Very slight diagonal and asymmetry like a person standing there with a normal camera on the grass. Bed surface low and close to the lawn, with a lightly uneven shallow compost edge feathering into tufts of grass in places, no boards or pavers round this bed. Timber planter stays in the left background, earth-stained older wood with a small dark gap and its short supporting legs underneath, not a new timber surround built into the ground. Leafy but with thin visible branches, plus taller irregular summer growth visible through reflections in the greenhouse. Preserve the area as one teaching bed with space to reach it; no other ground beds and no people.

Replace the ornamental repeated, colour-zoned rows in image 1 with a believable planting of the same veg at scale. Real loose lettuce foliage as in image 3, some slightly splayed, some lower and smaller after picking, two crowded heads overlapping, an older leaf lying against the compost, other leaves tipped sideways or out of view. Modestly sized groups of beetroot with mostly muted green leaves with thin reddish veins and small wine-dark stems near the soil, leaning into one another, some seen edge-on. Spinach further back in loose tussocks, a slightly thin or bolting plant among lower plants. Plants can be grouped in roughly planted rows, but there must be local overlaps and missing plants, one short sown run stops early, clumps break up the straight lines and different crops interlock a little. Leave real gaps of soil for legibility and access, including a picked-out patch. Unevenness comes from how plants grow and are harvested, not exaggerated rips or slug damage. Some leaves have soft drooping edges in shade, softer translucence in daylight, incidental recognisable stems at the crown behind neighbours. Keep small leaves and scale appropriate. Use the reference image's ordinary dark crumbly compost with a few short chopped woody fibres, compressed patches, small creases and scattered grass shoots along the edge. The lawn is a patchwork of subdued greens, a little straw-green at the most walked spot, here and there a low clover leaf, never perfectly sharp dense turf.

Photographic tone like the two real camera originals: daylight under bright cloud, a quiet soft highlight, believable contact shadows and local shade under the leaves, readable middle tones and slightly lower saturation. Real optical detail and ordinary distance softness, no texture enhancement, golden glow, dark vignette, glossy render or artificial blur. It should look like someone turned round in their own working garden and took a well exposed quick photo of the bed, with its season, layout and the full size clear enough for a small printed book.
